title: What is a hash value?
quick: A hash value is a short fixed-length fingerprint made from data by a hash function. If even one bit of the data changes, the hash changes, so hashes help show data is unchanged.

sections.title: How a hash works
text: A hash function reads any amount of data and produces a fixed-length result called a hash value or digest. The same data always gives the same hash. A tiny change in the data gives a very different hash.
You cannot rebuild the data from the hash. It is a fingerprint, not a compressed copy.

sections.title: Common algorithms
text: MD5 and SHA-1 are older. Researchers have shown that attackers can create two different inputs with the same hash for these, called a collision. SHA-256 belongs to the SHA-2 family defined by NIST in the Secure Hash Standard, and it is widely used now. Many labs record more than one algorithm. Follow your lab's own procedure.

sections.title: Uses in forensics
text: Hashes are used in several ways.
points: Check that an image matches the original drive
Check that a copy or export has not changed
Find known files, using hash sets such as the NSRL
Find exact copies of a file across a case

sections.title: Fuzzy hashes
text: A normal hash changes completely if one byte changes. A fuzzy hash, such as one made by ssdeep, gives a similarity score. It helps find files that are similar but not identical.

example: An examiner images a drive and the tool reports a SHA-256 hash for the drive. After copying the image to a server, the examiner hashes the copy. Both values match, so the copy is an exact copy of the image.
mistakes: Thinking a hash shows who made or changed a file.
Comparing only the first few characters of two hashes.
Hashing the wrong thing, such as a partition instead of the whole drive.
Using a hash made at one time to prove a file is unchanged without a record of when it was made.

terms.meaning: A method that turns any data into a fixed-length value.
Another word for the hash value.
Two different inputs that give the same hash.
A list of hashes of known files, used to include or filter files.

exam.q: Why does a matching hash show a copy is exact?
exam.a: Any change to the data would change the hash. So if both hashes are equal, the data is the same for practical purposes.

exam.q: Why is SHA-256 preferred to MD5 today?
exam.a: MD5 has known collisions, so it is weak for proving that data was not altered on purpose. SHA-256 has no known collisions.
